summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp/Python web application end to end: routes, views, the DAO/SQL layer, authentication/authorization utilities, session and template configuration, Jinja2 templates, and the DB/Redis service setup. The application is riddled with high-impact, reachable flaws: an unauthenticated SQL injection in student creation, global disabling of template auto-escaping leading to stored XSS, MD5 password hashing, CSRF protection commented out, session cookies without HttpOnly, and missing server-side authorization on all state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated attacker can inject SQL, store XSS that steals admin sessions (cookie is JS-readable), and perform admin-only actions directly. Coverage is the full repository except static vendor assets and the binary-flagged Dockerfile.app.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds its INSERT by interpolating the student name directly into the SQL text with Python %-formatting instead of using a bound parameter. The name originates from unauthenticated user input: views.students handles POST /students/ with no authorization check and passes data['name'] straight to Student.create (sqli/views.py:54-57, routes.py:13-14). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL by closing the quoted literal, e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE marks;-- , enabling data exfiltration (via stacked/boolean queries), modification, or destruction against the PostgreSQL backend. This is the canonical vulnerability of the app and is directly reachable by any anonymous visitor.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> cur.execute(q). Source: views.students POST -> Student.create(conn, data['name']). Contrast with the safe parameterized queries elsewhere (e.g. Course.create uses cur.execute(q, {'title': title, ...})).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query and let the driver bind the value: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/f-strings/concatenation from request data.

findings.title: Jinja2 auto-escaping globally disabled enabling stored/reflected XSS
findings.description: The Jinja2 environment is configured with autoescape=False, so every template expression renders HTML unescaped unless it explicitly adds the |e filter. Numerous templates emit attacker-controlled, persisted data without escaping, giving stored XSS. The strongest instance is course review text: any user can POST a review (POST /courses/{id}/review, no auth) with an HTML/script payload, which is stored and later rendered raw in course.jinja2:21 ({{ review.review_text }}). Other unescaped sinks fed by user input include course.jinja2:14-15 (course.title/description), courses.jinja2:17-18, students.jinja2:16, and the login error list in index.jinja2. Because the session cookie is also readable by JavaScript (HttpOnly=false), an injected script can steal an admin's session and fully take over the account.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: sqli/templates/course.jinja2:21 `{{ review.review_text }}` rendered without |e; review_text comes from Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) via views.review POST with no sanitization.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping: pass autoescape=True (or use jinja2.select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) to aiohttp_jinja2.setup, and remove reliance on manual |e. Keep |safe only for values proven to be trusted HTML.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 and compared non-constant-time
findings.description: check_password hashes the supplied password with a single round of unsalted MD5 and compares it to the stored hash. MD5 is cryptographically broken and extremely fast to brute-force; unsalted single-round hashes are trivially reversible with rainbow tables, so any disclosure of the users.pwd_hash column (e.g. via the SQL injection above) immediately yields plaintext passwords. The seed data confirms this scheme (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 stores md5('superadmin') etc.). The comparison also uses Python '==' on the hash, which is not constant-time (CWE-208), though that is secondary to the hashing weakness.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  (import: from hashlib import md5). Fixtures: pwd_hash = md5('superadmin') / md5('password').
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash such as Argon2id (argon2-cffi) or bcrypt, store the full algorithm/salt/parameters, and verify with the library's constant-time verify function. Migrate existing hashes on next login.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: A CSRF-checking middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates render a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware chain, so no CSRF validation ever runs. Combined with the cookie-based session, every state-changing POST (login, logout, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks) is vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker page can silently submit these forms using a victim's authenticated session. For an admin victim this allows forced course/mark creation; for any visitor it allows forced login/logout and data creation.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,  error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware factory (middlewares.py:26) is never referenced in the active list.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable a CSRF middleware in the chain and enforce token checks on all unsafe methods. Fix the token comparison to be constant-time, and pair with SameSite cookies. Also note middlewares.py:32 compares tokens with != (non-constant-time) and should use hmac.compare_digest.

findings.title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints
findings.description: Authorization is enforced only in the UI (templates hide forms behind {% if auth_user.is_admin %}), not on the server. The evaluate handler, which assigns student marks and is presented as an admin-only action, has no @authorize decorator and no is_admin check, so any unauthenticated client can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to create marks. The same missing-authorization flaw affects views.students POST (create student, views.py:54-57), views.courses POST (create course, views.py:86-90), and views.review POST (create review, views.py:119-130) — all reachable without authentication. The authorize() decorator (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) exists but is applied only to logout.
findings.evidence: @template('evaluate.jinja2') async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) — no get_auth_user/authorize call. Route POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} (routes.py:21-23). UI gate only: course.jinja2:41 `{% if auth_user.is_admin %}`.
findings.recommendation: Apply server-side authorization to every state-changing handler: decorate with @authorize() (and @authorize(ensure_admin=True) for admin-only actions like evaluate and course creation), and verify permissions on the server regardless of what the UI shows.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly (and without Secure)
findings.description: The Redis session storage is constructed with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS reachable through course reviews (and the globally disabled auto-escaping), an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate an administrator's session, converting XSS into full account takeover. No Secure flag is set either, so the cookie can traverse plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Construct RedisStorage with httponly=True and secure=True (serve over HTTPS), and set samesite='Lax'/'Strict'. There is no legitimate reason for the session cookie to be script-accessible.

findings.title: aiohttp application debug mode enabled in production path
findings.description: The Application is created with debug=True, and the error templates render exception internals to the client (errors/50x.jinja2:6 renders error.__dict__). Together these can disclose stack traces, internal object state, and configuration details to attackers, aiding further exploitation. run.py also sets logging level to DEBUG globally.
findings.evidence:
app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...]). Error template: `
{{ error.__dict__ }}
` in sqli/templates/errors/50x.jinja2.
findings.recommendation: Disable debug mode in deployed environments (drive it from config/env), and never render exception internals (error.__dict__, stack traces) to clients — log them server-side and show a generic error page.
